A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same City-Networks dataset and Jacobian-based measurements. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and retained equations, tables and figures can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v2 reports original GNN and graph-transformer benchmarks, influence measurements and ablation results in Sections 3–4 and Appendices B–C.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds travel-time labeling, coordinate controls, deeper-model experiments, RingTransfer evaluation and additional heterophilic datasets.

M1.justification: The main dataset construction, 16-hop quantile labels and definitions of Jacobian influence, total influence and R remain unchanged. The travel-time experiment applies the existing weighted-eccentricity formula to alternative targets; it does not introduce a new learning algorithm or influence-aggregation procedure.

E1.justification: v3 retains the original coverage and adds RingTransfer source-to-target prediction, Roman-Empire, Wisconsin, Texas and Cornell, plus Paris accessibility prediction using estimated travel-time labels (Appendices C.2, D.4–D.5). These substantially expand the evaluated data and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 Table 5 and v3 Table 2 contain the same ten baselines, including ChebNet and DropEdge, which are not new additions. The original influence comparison also retains its six models. Added experiments use existing models without replacing comparator membership in the retained comparisons.

E3.justification: v3 adds coordinate-masked and coordinate-only controls, extends depth testing through 48 and 64 layers, and measures influence in 64-layer models. RingTransfer introduces 16-node rings, 5k/1k/1k training/validation/test graphs, 8- and 16-layer models, and target-node-only influence evaluation. The original city splits, training budget and hyperparameter search remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 already contains labeling-range, hidden-width and neighborhood-sampling ablations, including a 32-layer Paris GCN test. v3 adds coordinate reliance controls, travel-time labeling sensitivity, broader experiments beyond the task range, and RingTransfer architectural diagnostics (Table 5; Figures 6 and 12–14). These investigate spatial shortcuts, depth-related failure and model-dependent influence patterns.

E5.justification: The existing five-run, different-seed reporting of means and standard deviations is retained. New accuracy entries use the established uncertainty format, while influence tables continue reporting point estimates. No new uncertainty-estimation procedure, significance test or explicit increase in repeated runs is reported.

E6.justification: Original benchmark tables and figure artwork retain their results, while v3 adds substantial new outcomes. Table 5 reports Paris GCN accuracy of 51.4±0.4 with coordinates masked; RingTransfer achieves 100% accuracy for all three evaluated models, with R=5.27, 5.21 and 3.34 for GCN, GraphSAGE and Exphormer. New depth results show deterioration beyond 16 layers. However, Paris GCN at 32 layers is approximately 50% in new Figure 12 versus 53% in retained Figure 9, without an explained setting difference.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, Equations 1–61, propositions, theorems and proofs are retained after matching appendix renumbering. New Appendix G.4 qualifies the interpretation of the spectral bound and its relationship to prior work; it supplies no new formal result or revised proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the central claims concerning a large transductive benchmark, per-hop Jacobian diagnostics, empirical validation and theoretical justification. Replacing 'model-agnostic' with 'generic' clarifies applicability across differentiable architectures; v2 already explicitly acknowledges that the measured values are model-dependent.

C2.justification: Beyond v2's model-dependence, computational-cost and cancellation caveats, v3 explains how architectural bias can distort estimates of the true task range. It also interprets RingTransfer behavior through architectural shortcuts, qualifies transportation realism, and explains that the spectral bound need not be tight and low maximum degree does not necessarily imply sparsity (Appendices C.2, D.4, F and G.4).

D1.justification: Appendix A specifies PyG 2.7.0 and the total_influence API, replacing the less precise 'latest version' and 'Total Influence' descriptions. v3 documents the travel-time weighting recipe, while retaining the repository, feature-processing instructions, training search space and computational details. It drops v2's explicit note about GraphGPS exhausting 48GB even with hidden_size=16 at 16 layers.

R1.justification: Where v2 describes R as similar to Bamberger et al. (2025), v3 explicitly identifies it as a shortest-path instance of that measurement and emphasizes the per-hop diagnostic contribution. Focused new discussions cite work on heterophily evaluation and contrast the spectral analysis with Jamadandi et al. (2024), without broadly restructuring the research positioning.

P1.justification: The seven main sections and most existing prose remain intact. v3 selectively revises the introduction and measurement discussion, expands appendix subsections, moves availability information into Appendix A and the baseline summary into Section 3, and adds acknowledgment and contact text. This is limited restructuring rather than an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: Five new figures (6 and 12–15) and three new tables (5, 7 and 8) substantially extend the presentation of experimental evidence. The original baseline table moves from the appendix to the main text as Table 2. Existing figure artwork is retained, while the ICLR template changes headers, typography and placement throughout.

improvement.justification: The coordinate controls, additional diagnostics and explicit qualifications about model bias, transportation realism and prior-work overlap strengthen support and interpretation of the existing contribution. The gain is limited by an unexplained difference between the retained and new Paris GCN depth plots: approximately 53% versus 50% at 32 layers for the stated 16-hop task. Overall, the additional validation and clearer scope provide a useful but bounded quality improvement.
